title: Development of a Quantitative Contrast CT-Based TAVR-Risk Score to Reliably Predict Deformation in Bicuspid Aortic Valves.
authors: Kazuki Suruga; Vivek Patel; Hasan Jilaihawi; Hidemasa Shitan; Tej Sheth; Yuchao Guo; Takashi Nagasaka; Daniel Ng; Tarun Chakravarty; Wen Cheng; Yuito Okada; Aakriti Gupta; Mamoo Nakamura; Raj R Makkar
abstract:
Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) calcification affects clinical outcomes by causing transcatheter heart valve (THV) deformation after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). However, a computed tomography (CT)-based scoring system for grading BAV calcification severity and predicting THV deformation has not been established.
This study sought to develop a cardiac CT-based BAV TAVR-risk score for grading BAV calcification severity and predicting THV deformation.
This single-center retrospective study included consecutive patients with BAV who underwent TAVR using contemporary balloon-expandable valves between January 2016 and December 2024 and who had preprocedural and postprocedural CT imaging. The BAV TAVR-risk score integrated calcification severity and distribution across valve leaflets, raphe, annulus, and left ventricular outflow tract, quantified using a fixed HU-850 threshold of detection on contrast-enhanced CT scans. Score thresholds were derived by receiver operating curve analysis with Youden index optimization. Patients were categorized into low-, intermediate-, and high-risk score groups.
Among 321 patients (median follow-up: 1,825 days; Q1-Q3: 765-1,825 days), 56 (17.4%) were classified into the high-risk score group. Both underexpansion and eccentricity of the THV occurred in 49 of the 321 patients (15.3%) and were predominantly observed in the high-risk score group. However, in the low-risk score group, 149 of 155 patients (96.1%) demonstrated no underexpansion or eccentricity of the THV. A high BAV TAVR-risk score independently predicted both underexpansion and eccentricity of the THV (OR: 89.13; 95% CI: 35.02-226.83; P < 0.001).
This CT-based BAV TAVR-risk score provides a systematic method to precisely quantify BAV severity which reliably predicts THV deformation for BAV patients with contemporary balloon-expandable valves and may help guide decision-making in this challenging population.

title: Transcatheter vs Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement for Isolated Native Aortic Regurgitation: National Propensity-Matched Analysis.
authors: Yukari Kobayashi; Afek Kodesh; Maria C Alu; Alexandra Popma; David J Cohen; Martin B Leon; Juan F Granada; Jeffrey J Popma; Harun Kundi
abstract:
Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) is well established for aortic stenosis, while its application for isolated native aortic regurgitation (AR) was previously off label and technically challenging. Comparative data between TAVR and surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) are limited.
The aim of this study was to compare patient characteristics and outcomes of off-label TAVR vs SAVR among patients with isolated native AR.
Using the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Medicare Provider Analysis and Review database, patients ≥65 years of age who underwent TAVR or SAVR for isolated native AR (2017-2023) were identified. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed to evaluate short- and long-term outcomes. Fine-Gray models accounted for death as a competing risk, reported as subdistribution HRs (SHRs).
Among 9,859 patients, 1,742 propensity score-matched pairs were included, with balanced baseline characteristics (mean age 75.8 years vs 75.7 years; female sex 517 of 1,742 [29.7%] vs 528 of 1,742 [30.3%]). In the matched cohort, TAVR was associated with shorter hospitalization (OR: 0.33; 95% CI: 0.28-0.39; P < 0.001) and lower in-hospital mortality (OR: 0.62; 95% CI: 0.39-1.00; P = 0.048) but higher 30-day pacemaker implantation (OR: 1.73; 95% CI: 1.33-2.25; P < 0.001). Through 5 years (median follow-up 2.58 years), TAVR was associated with increased repeat aortic valve replacement (SHR: 2.04; 95% CI: 1.13-3.66) but similar all-cause mortality (HR: 1.14; 95% CI: 0.98-1.31) and heart failure-related readmission (SHR: 1.09; 95% CI: 0.98-1.21) between treatment strategies.
In this analysis, TAVR was associated with shorter hospitalization and comparable 5-year survival as SAVR, although pacemaker and long-term reinterventions rates were higher.

title: Prognostic Impact of Paravalvular Regurgitation in Patients With Severe Low-Flow, Low-Gradient Aortic Stenosis Undergoing TAVR.
authors: Michele Bellino; Angelo Silverio; Germano Junior Ferruzzi; Francesco Saia; Antonio Giulio Bruno; Paride Boragine; Andrea Buono; Maria Luisa De Rosa; Francesco Paolo Cancro; Italo Porto; Gabriele Crimi; Paolo Calabrò; Elisabetta Moscarella; Alfonso Ielasi; Carolina Montonati; Marco De Carlo; Alessandro Sticchi; Francesca Lanni; Luca Esposito; Francesca Maria Di Muro; Francesco Maiellaro; Ivan Francesco Calchera; Giacomo Boccuzzi; Antonio Sorropago; Fernando Scudiero; Tiziana Attisano; Rodolfo Citro; Giovanni Granata; Giuseppe De Luca; Carmine Vecchione; Giuseppe Musumeci; Gennaro Galasso; LOW-TAVR Investigators
abstract:
Paravalvular regurgitation (PVR) is a frequent complication after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) and may influence clinical outcomes in patients with high-gradient aortic stenosis. However, its prognostic relevance in patients with low-flow, low-gradient aortic stenosis (LFLG-AS) undergoing TAVR remains incompletely elucidated.
This study sought to evaluate the prognostic significance of PVR severity in patients with LFLG-AS undergoing TAVR with current-generation prostheses.
This multicenter registry-based cohort study included consecutive patients with LFLG-AS undergoing TAVR from January 2019 to December 2024 at 17 high-volume Italian centers. PVR severity was classified using a 5-class grading scheme and stratified as <2+ (none/trace or mild) or ≥2+ (mild-moderate or worse) based on separation of Kaplan-Meier curves for the primary outcome. The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause death and heart failure hospitalization up to 2 years. Propensity score-weighted Cox regression was used to estimate the independent impact of PVR severity on clinical outcomes.
A total of 1,358 patients were included. Kaplan-Meier analysis showed lower event-free survival among patients with ≥2+ PVR at discharge compared with those with <2+ PVR. After propensity score weighting, PVR ≥2+ was independently associated with a higher risk of the primary endpoint (adjusted HR: 3.77; 95% CI: 2.88-4.95), as well as higher risks of all-cause death, mainly cardiovascular, and heart failure hospitalization. These findings were consistent across both classical and paradoxical LFLG-AS phenotypes.
In this large, real-world study of patients with LFLG-AS treated with current-generation TAVR devices, PVR ≥2+ was independently associated with worse clinical outcomes after discharge, regardless of LFLG-AS subtype.

title: Prevalence and Consequences of Guideline-Directed Indications for Aortic Valve Replacement in the EARLY TAVR Trial.
authors: Mahesh V Madhavan; Allan Schwartz; Brian R Lindman; Philippe Pibarot; David J Cohen; J Bradley Oldemeyer; Vasilis Babaliaros; William F Fearon; David Daniels; Adnan Chhatriwalla; Clifford J Kavinsky; Pinak Shah; Molly Szerlip; Thom Dahle; Kashish Goel; William O'Neill; Raj Makkar; Charles Davidson; Tej Sheth; Paul Sorajja; James DeVries; Jeffrey Southard; Jeremiah P Depta; Andrei Pop; Rebbecca T Hahn; Yanglu Zhao; Martin B Leon; Philippe Genereux; EARLY TAVR Trial Executive Committee and Study Investigators
abstract:
The current American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association valvular heart disease guidelines were published before several recent trials that provide greater support for early intervention in patients with asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis (AS).
This study sought to investigate the prevalence and clinical impact of American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Class II recommendations for AVR in the EARLY TAVR trial.
The EARLY TAVR trial randomized patients with asymptomatic severe AS to transfemoral transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) with a balloon-expandable valve or clinical surveillance (CS) with conversion to TAVR based on development of ACC/AHA Class I indications. Patients in the intention-to-treat cohort were stratified by presence of a Class II indication for AVR at randomization. The primary endpoint of the present analysis was the composite of all-cause death, stroke, or heart failure hospitalization. Interaction tests were performed to assess whether the treatment effect differed by level of guideline recommendation. Timing of conversion to AVR in the CS group according to the presence/absence of Class II indications was also assessed.
Of the 901 patients randomized to TAVR (N = 445) and CS (N = 446), 636 (70.6%) patients had no guideline recommendation, and 265 (29.4%) had at least1 1 Class II recommendation for AVR at the time of randomization. At a median follow-up of 3.8 years, patients with a Class II indication for AVR experienced higher rates of the primary endpoint (Class II: 24.5% vs no recommendation: 14.5%; HR = 1.78; 95% CI: 1.30-2.44; P < 0.001) and were more likely to have acute valve syndrome at the time of conversion. Compared with CS, the relative benefit of early TAVR on the primary endpoint was similar regardless of the presence or absence of a Class II guideline recommendation (HR = 0.62; 95% CI: 0.37-1.02 vs 0.61; 95% CI: 0.40-0.92; Pinteraction = 0.96).
Among patients in the EARLY TAVR trial, Class II indications for AVR were present in almost one-third of patients at baseline. The benefit of early TAVR was consistent regardless of the presence or absence of Class II indications. These findings support the strategy of early TAVR over CS in asymptomatic patients with severe AS, independent of guideline indications.

title: Prosthesis-Patient Mismatch and Patient-Centered Outcomes After TAVR.
authors: Ottavia Cozzi; Daijiro Tomii; Jonas Lanz; Holger Thiele; Dik Heg; Michael Joner; Helge Möllmann; Axel Linke; Lenard Conradi; Stefan Toggweiler; Christian Thilo; Bernard Prendergast; Stephan Windecker; Thomas Pilgrim; SCOPE I Investigators
abstract:
Prosthesis-patient mismatch (PPM) after transcatheter aortic valve replacement has been widely studied for its association with clinical outcomes, but its effect on patient-reported health status remains less defined.
This study sought to evaluate the association between PPM severity and health status through 3-year follow-up after transcatheter aortic valve replacement.
This post hoc analysis of the SCOPE I (Safety and Efficacy of the ACURATE Neo/TF Compared to the SAPIEN 3 Bioprosthesis) randomized trial categorized patients according to PPM severity using Valve Academic Research Consortium-3 criteria. Endpoints included survival and patient-reported health status, with an integrated outcome defined as being alive with good health status (Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Overall Summary score ≥75 without a decline of >10 points from baseline).
Among 662 patients, moderate and severe PPM occurred in 184 (27.8%) and 69 (10.4%), respectively. All-cause mortality at 1 and 3 years was 7.0% and 20.5%, with no differences across PPM categories. Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Overall Summary score was similar through 1 year but lower at 3 years in patients with severe vs no PPM (median 71.1 vs 83.9; P = 0.027). Fewer patients with severe PPM were alive with good health status at 3 years (30.6% vs 49.4%; P = 0.021). In multivariable analysis, severe PPM was associated with a lower likelihood of the integrated outcome (OR: 0.51; 95% CI: 0.27-0.96; P = 0.036), but this association was no longer statistically significant after adjustment for 30-day mitral regurgitation (OR: 0.59; 95% CI: 0.30-1.15; P = 0.121).
Among survivors, severe PPM was associated with a lower likelihood of good health status at 3 years. This association was attenuated after accounting for 30-day residual mitral regurgitation, suggesting a possible contributory role. Given the post hoc design, the findings are hypothesis-generating.

title: Cardiac Damage and Clinical Outcomes in Symptomatic Severe Aortic Stenosis Undergoing Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement.
authors: Akihiro Tobe; Michele Gallazzi; Niels van Royen; Ignacio J Amat-Santos; Martin Hudec; Matjaz Bunc; Ben J L Van den Branden; Peep Laanmets; Daniel Unic; Bela Merkely; Renicus S Hermanides; Vlasis Ninios; Marcin Protasiewicz; Benno J W M Rensing; Pedro L Martin; Fausto Feres; Manuel De Sousa Almeida; Eric van Belle; Axel Linke; Alfonso Ielasi; Matteo Montorfano; Mark Webster; Konstantinos Toutouzas; Emmanuel Teiger; Francesco Bedogni; Michiel Voskuil; Manuel Pan; Oskar Angerås; Won-Keun Kim; Jürgen Rothe; Mohamed Abdel-Wahab; Ivica Kristić; Vicente Peral; Scot Garg; Ashokkumar Thakkar; Udita Chandra; Pieter C Smits; Daniele Andreini; Philippe Généreux; Marie-Claude Morice; Andreas Baumbach; Patrick W Serruys; Yoshinobu Onuma
abstract:
The extent of cardiac damage in patients with aortic stenosis (AS) is associated with worse clinical outcomes.
This study sought to investigate the clinical impact of cardiac damage using the updated criteria incorporating the echocardiographic probability of pulmonary hypertension.
This post hoc subanalysis of LANDMARK trial, which randomized 768 patients with severe AS to the Myval transcatheter heart valve (THV) series or to contemporary THVs (Sapien and Evolut series), used updated cardiac damage classification: stage 0, no cardiac damage; stage 1, left ventricular damage; stage 2, left atrial or mitral valve damage; stage 3, pulmonary artery or tricuspid valve damage; and stage 4, right ventricular damage. The impact of cumulative cardiac damage, defined as meeting all criteria for stages 1 to 4, was also assessed. The primary endpoint was 1-year all-cause mortality.
Cardiac damage stages were assessed in 596 patients (stage 0, n = 36; stage 1, n = 88; stage 2, n = 284; stage 3, n = 84; stage 4, n = 104), with a mean age of 80.2 (5.7) years and a mean Society of Thoracic Surgeons score of 3.3% (2.4%). One-year mortality was 0%, 1.1%, 4.7%, 7.2%, and 20.4% in stages 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4, respectively (log-rank P < 0.001). The area under the curve for predicting 1-year mortality was 0.739. Patients with cumulative cardiac damage had the highest mortality (23.6%). In the multivariable analysis, stage 4 was independently associated with higher 1-year mortality.
The updated cardiac damage staging stratified 1-year mortality after transcatheter aortic valve replacement, highlighting the importance of comprehensive echocardiographic assessment in severe AS. (LANDMARK Trial: a Randomised Controlled Trial of Myval THV [LANDMARK]; NCT04275726).

title: Valvular Shock in the Cardiac Intensive Care Unit: Perioperative Care for Transcatheter Valve Interventions.
authors: Graeme Prosperi-Porta; Garima Dahiya; Benjamin Hibbert; Jacob C Jentzer
abstract: Valvular heart disease is an uncommon but high-risk cause of cardiogenic shock requiring rapid, multidisciplinary management aimed at bridging patients to definitive surgical or transcatheter valve intervention. Early comprehensive Doppler echocardiography is essential, as clinical signs may be subtle. Distinguishing decompensated chronic valvular disease from acute unstable lesions guides urgency and treatment strategy. Medical stabilization and mechanical circulatory support vary markedly between stenotic and regurgitant lesions, and standard shock therapies may be harmful in specific contexts. Transcatheter approaches are preferred when feasible, though their expanding use introduces added complexity in cardiac intensive care.

title: Coronary Risk in Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement, Overview of Data, Challenges, and Best Practices.
authors: Louay Dandach; Khalil Mahmoudi; Maroun Sfeir; Alaa Masri
abstract: Coronary artery obstruction is a rare complication of transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). This risk increases in TAVR-valve-in-valve procedure. Several anatomic risk factors were described in many studies to identify the predictive elements of coronary artery occlusion on computed tomography cardiac scan. Rescue percutaneous coronary intervention was the first approach described to treat this complication with a high mortality rate. Later on, preventive chimney stenting technique was evaluated and results showed that is a safe and effective strategy but it leads to a difficult coronary access later. New preventive techniques are being evaluated recently (Basilica and Shorctut).

title: Coronary Artery Revascularization in Patients Undergoing Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement.
authors: Stephen McHugh; Haytham Allaham; Diljon Chahal; Anuj Gupta
abstract: Patients with concomitant severe aortic stenosis and significant coronary artery disease present a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge in clinical practice. There are no clear-cut guidelines as to the timing of revascularization in these patients who are referred for transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). This article aims to show that in patients without high-grade proximal coronary artery disease, revascularization after TAVR is safe, feasible, and practical. Additionally, the use of preoperative TAVR computed tomographic angiography might be used in both intermediate and high-risk patients rather than invasive coronary angiography to assess for significant proximal coronary artery disease to help guide the timing of revascularization.

title: The spectrum of amyloid cardiovascular disease.
authors: Filippos Triposkiadis; Randall C Starling; Mazen Hanna; Andrew Xanthopoulos
abstract: Cardiac amyloidosis, historically characterized as a restrictive cardiomyopathy, is now understood as a multi-compartmental disorder. Atrial amyloid infiltration-whether ANP-derived isolated atrial amyloidosis secondary to atrial stretch, or primary atrial ATTR infiltration-produces an atrial cardiomyopathy that frequently manifests as atrial fibrillation and a thrombogenic substrate even in sinus rhythm. Cardiac amyloidosis exhibits a high prevalence in heart failure, particularly among elderly patients presenting with preserved ejection fraction. Furthermore, TTR amyloid frequently coexists with degenerative aortic stenosis, and amyloid deposits are also found in the coronary microcirculation and the aorta. Given the current availability of efficacious treatments for amyloidosis, the recognition of these diverse clinical manifestations is paramount for achieving accurate diagnosis, appropriate risk stratification, and timely therapeutic intervention to enhance cardiovascular outcomes. This review frames amyloid cardiovascular disease as a multisystem process affecting the myocardium, atria, valves, and vasculature-often with extracardiac red flags-rather than solely as an infiltrative ventricular cardiomyopathy. Actionable implications currently concentrate on ventricular ATTR/AL cardiomyopathy and concomitant aortic stenosis; coronary and aortic medial deposits remain mechanistically important research targets rather than independently treatable lesions.

title: Intravascular lithotripsy for calcific stenosis of the abdominal aorta in a patient with Takayasu arteritis.
authors: John H Cabot; Mary Cain; Arash Fereydooni; Michael D Sgroi
journal: Journal of vascular surgery cases and innovative techniques
abstract: Takayasu arteritis is a rare large-vessel vasculitis that predominantly affects the aorta and its major branches. Although stenotic lesions and fibrotic wall thickening are common, extensive aortic calcification with mesenteric involvement is exceedingly rare. Diffuse calcification of the aorta poses significant challenges for both open and endovascular treatment. We report the case of Takayasu arteritis with near-circumferential calcification of the entire aorta and most visceral branches, successfully managed with intravascular lithotripsy.

title: Novel endovascular management of a displaced aortic endograft component during transcatheter aortic valve replacement.
authors: Punit Vyas; Grant Woodruff; Andre Hall; Kashish Goel; Brian Lima; John Curci
journal: Journal of vascular surgery cases and innovative techniques
abstract: We report the case of a 73-year-old man with prior endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) of the abdominal aorta complicated by type Ia endoleak requiring two proximal aortic cuffs. Ten years later, he underwent transfemoral transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) for severe aortic stenosis. During the delivery of the transcatheter aortic valve replacement device, one of the aortic cuffs was displaced into the distal thoracic aorta. This case report describes a rare complication of delayed device displacement during TAVR and demonstrates a novel strategy for endovascular salvage. It highlights the opportunity for endovascular repair during TAVR planning in patients with prior aortic stent grafts. In addition, close multidisciplinary collaboration is valuable for managing unexpected device interactions.

title: Association between biological age acceleration and the risk of aortic valve stenosis: An observational epidemiologic and Mendelian randomization study.
authors: Yiqi Zheng; Xinghao Xu; Ruijie Li; Zhenyu Xiong; Han Wen; Yue Guo; Menghui Liu; Huimin Zhou; Xingfeng Xu; Shaozhao Zhang; Rihua Huang; Zezhi Ke; Zihao Huang; Jiayuan Zhang; Xiaodong Zhuang; Xinxue Liao
journal: The journal of nutrition, health & aging
abstract:
Biological age acceleration (BAA) is thought to be a major risk factor for age-related diseases, but its role in aortic valve stenosis (AVS) remains uncertain. We aimed to assess the associations between biological aging and the risk of AVS.
This study involved 4526 participants from the Real-world Data of Cardiometabolic Protection (RED-CARPET) study and 5114 participants from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) study. BAA was assessed using clinical biomarkers through the Klemera-Doubal method (KDM) and the PhenoAge algorithm. We employed multivariable logistic regression and restricted cubic spline (RCS) regression to examine the association between BAA and AVS risk. Additionally, Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis was conducted to assess causality.
In the RED-CARPET cohort of 4526 participants (mean age 60.93 years, 33.5% female), 113 AVS events were recorded. In the ARIC cohort of 5114 participants (mean age 51.94 years, 56.4% female, 82.3% White), there were 266 AVS events. After fully adjusting for confounding variables, each standard deviation increase in BAA was significantly associated with elevated AVS risk (RED-CARPET: KDM-BA acceleration: OR 1.29, 95% CI 1.07-1.55; PhenoAge acceleration: OR 1.48, 95% CI 1.24-1.77; ARIC: KDM-BA acceleration: OR 1.42, 95% CI 1.24-1.63; PhenoAge acceleration: OR 1.30, 95% CI 1.11-1.51). The RCS regression model revealed significant linear relationships between BAA and the risk of AVS in both cohorts. MR analysis suggested a potential causal relationship between KDM-BA acceleration and AVS risk (OR 1.38, 95% CI 1.21-1.57).
BAA, as derived from clinical biomarkers, is independently associated with an increased risk of AVS. This finding suggests that BAA, as a composite indicator of systemic biological aging, may complement traditional risk factors in the early identification of high-risk populations for AVS, and offer the possibility of early intervention for prevention.

title: Ultra-high-pitch photon-counting computed tomography (PCCT) versus ultra-high-pitch dual-source computed tomography (DSCT) for coronary artery disease evaluation in transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) patients.
authors: Ines Mecking; Marc von der Stück; Eric Corban; Michael Frick; Jörg Schröder; Roman Iwa; Christiane K Kuhl; Timm Dirrichs
abstract:
To compare radiation dose and image quality of coronary artery reconstructions obtained from non-coronary-dedicated transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) planning CT scans using ultra-high-pitch photon-counting CT (PCCT) and ultra-high-pitch energy-integrating detector dual-source CT (EID-DSCT; hereafter referred to as DSCT), including assessment of the feasibility of coronary artery evaluation according to the Coronary Artery Disease Reporting and Data System (CAD-RADS).
Retrospective study on consecutive patients with aortic valve stenosis (AS) undergoing contrast-enhanced TAVI planning CT, either PCCT or DSCT between August 2021 and June 2023. CT dose index (CTDI) and dose length product (DLP) were used to calculate the effective radiation dose (eRD). Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) were calculated using standardized region-of-interest (ROI) analysis. Coronary arteries were evaluated by three independent radiologists using 5-point Likert scales followed by a classification according to the CAD-RADS system.
187 patients (83 female, median age 82, IQR: 76-84) underwent 190 CT-examinations, 103 PCCT (54.2%) and 87 (45.8%) DSCT. Three patients underwent both PCCT and DSCT for clinical reasons. Mean CTDI and DLP were significantly lower in PCCT compared to DSCT (21.9 vs. 52.8 and 607.9 vs. 906.8, respectively; both p < 0.001), with a correspondingly lower mean effective radiation dose (eRD) in PCCT compared to DSCT (10.3 ± 5.4 mSv vs. 15.4 ± 5.6 mSv, p < 0.001). While both SNR and CNR were lower in PCCT than in DSCT (SNR: 35.28 ± 11.63 in PCCT vs. 45.6 ± 16.3 in DSCT, p < 0.001; CNR: 49.25 ± 13.31 in PCCT vs. 57.42 v ± 22.55 in DSCT, p = 0.004), PCCT outperformed DSCT in every one of the eleven visual image categories. Overall image quality was rated as good or excellent in 71.8% (74/103) of PCCT vs. 19.5% (17/87) of DSCT scans. Coronary reconstructions were rated as good or excellent in 72.8% (75/103) of PCCT vs. 20.7% of DSCT datasets. CAD-RADS [1-5] rating was possible in 68.9% (71/103) of PCCT vs. 39.1% (34/87) of DSCT datasets.
Photon-counting computed tomography (PCCT) allows for significantly improved assessability of the coronary arteries in TAVI planning CT compared with dual-source CT (DSCT), while achieving a substantially lower radiation dose.

title: Association between early vein graft failure and long-term major adverse cardiovascular events following off-pump coronary artery bypass grafting: an exploratory retrospective cohort study.
authors: Zhaoxi Qi; Yunpeng Zhu; Xiaofeng Ye; Zhe Wang; Sigrid E Sandner; Yi Yang; Qiang Zhao
abstract:
Early vein graft failure (VGF) following coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) is far from rare and often clinically silent. While mid-to-late graft failure is established to predict adverse clinical events, the long-term prognostic impact of predischarge early VGF remains poorly defined. This study aimed to evaluate the association between early VGF and 10-year clinical outcomes following off-pump CABG.
In this exploratory retrospective cohort study, adult patients undergoing elective isolated off-pump CABG using vein grafts with early postoperative coronary computed tomography angiography between July 2014 and December 2015 were consecutively included. Baseline, intraoperative, and postoperative data were collected from electronic medical records. VGF was defined as Fitzgibbon grade B (≥50% stenosis) or O (occlusion). Patients were stratified into the early VGF group (with at least one failed vein graft) and non-early VGF group (without failed vein grafts). Clinical follow-up was conducted through routine outpatient visits or standardized telephone interviews in accordance with institutional protocol. Primary outcomes included 10-year major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE, composite of all-cause death, myocardial infarction, stroke, or revascularization) and its individual components. Secondary outcomes included perioperative myocardial injury and perioperative myocardial infarction (PMI). Propensity score overlap weighting was applied to adjust for baseline confounders. Exploratory post-hoc landmark and piecewise Cox analyses were performed to address non-proportional hazards.
A total of 233 patients were included in the analyses (mean age 64.3±7.5 years; 18.4% female). Among them, early VGF was identified in 33 (14.2%) patients and 41 (5.9%) vein grafts. Early VGF numerically increased the risk of perioperative myocardial injury [45.5% vs. 30.5%, odds ratio (OR) 1.90, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.89-4.01; P=0.09] and PMI (12.1% vs. 6.0%, OR 2.16, 95% CI: 0.57-6.69; P=0.21), though without statistical significance. Over a median follow-up of 9.6 years, there was no statistically significant difference in 10-year MACE between the two groups [early VGF 51.5% vs. non-early VGF 48.2%; adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) 1.31, 95% CI: 0.76-2.24; P=0.33]. In exploratory landmark analyses addressing non-proportional hazards (P=0.03), early VGF was associated with a higher risk of MACE within the first 2 years post-surgery (aHR 2.18, 95% CI: 1.14-4.17; P=0.02), which attenuated beyond the 2-year landmark (aHR 0.56, 95% CI: 0.22-1.46; P=0.24). Additionally, early VGF was associated with a higher risk of repeat revascularization (18.2% vs. 7.7%; aHR 3.06, 95% CI: 1.13-8.31; P=0.03).
Predischarge early VGF was not significantly associated with the overall 10-year risk of MACE following off-pump CABG. Exploratory findings regarding early risk clustering within 2 years and an increased risk of repeat revascularization remain hypothesis-generating. Further prospective studies are warranted to validate these observations.

title: RELATION OF HEART WEIGHT WITH AGE AND WEIGHT OF CADAVER

abstract: Introduction: Height, weight, and age of person has significant impact on the normal size of heart. These parameters need to be considered when cut-off values indicating the need for treatment or even surgery are established. The aim of present work is to study the relation of weight of the heart with age and weight of cadaver. Material and Methods: The study was performed in the Department of Anatomy, Shri Ram Murti Smarak Institute of Medical Sciences, Bareilly on 30 hearts from embalmed cadavers. The hearts were procured from the cadavers available in our department. The heart was thoroughly cleaned and measurements were taken. Results: The mean heart weight was 223.37 ± 57.78 g. Significant relationship between age of the cadaver and weight of the heart (p=0.0004), weight of cadaver and weight of heart (p=0.0001) was observed. Conclusion: The above study provides valuable data of the heart in our geographical location, which may be useful for cardiac surgeons and physicians.

title: Understanding pedagogical challenges faced by technology teachers in special needs classrooms
authors: Katane Elizabeth Kekana; Thokozani Isaac Mtshali
journal: Journal of Education and Learning Technology
abstract: Teaching learners with special educational needs requires dynamic and adaptive pedagogical strategies that can lead to social development and academic success. This can be possible if teachers are assisted in mitigating the daily challenges of teaching such learners. This qualitative exploratory case study investigated the pedagogical challenges encountered by two Grade 9 Technology teachers in the Capricorn District of Limpopo Province. This study used Shulman’s Content and Pedagogical Knowledge framework to understand teachers’ challenges. Data was collected through semi-structured interviews and classroom observations; all collected data were analysed thematically. This study found that teachers experienced various challenges, including the emotional labour of teaching, burnout in the LSEN environment and the enactment of instructional knowledge. The study concluded that the sampled teachers displayed weaknesses in lesson planning, activating learners’ prior knowledge, diagnosing errors, achieving curriculum objectives and sustaining engagement. As a result, it was recommended that support through teacher assistants, creative differentiated strategies and enhanced digital-technology literacy to improve outcomes for learners with special needs was imminent.

title: Integration of Biomechanics and Digital Technology: Using Kinovea for Motion Analysis and Learning for Beginner Athletes
authors: Muhammad Nur Hudha; Riezky Maya Probosari; Annisa Nur Khasanah; Supurwoko; Salsabila Kholifahtun Nisa’; Gifran Rihla Gifarka Latief
journal: Journal of Coaching and Sports Science
abstract: Background: The integration of biomechanics with digital motion-analysis technologies has introduced new approaches for examining movement efficiency, kinematic characteristics, and technical patterns in walking and running activities. Kinovea, as an accessible motion-analysis software, provides both visual and quantitative feedback. However, its application in supporting technique development among beginner athletes remains insufficiently explored. Aim: This study aims to describe the use of Kinovea in biomechanics training and examine its contribution to the awareness of kinematic characteristics and movement techniques among beginner athletes. Methods: A descriptive qualitative design involved 72 beginner athletes aged 18–25 years selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected over 16 weeks through interviews, field observations, and motion video recordings analyzed using Kinovea. Kinematic data focused on joint angles, stride behavior, and movement phases during walking, running, and the flight phase. Qualitative data were analyzed using content analysis with NVivo 12, while kinematic results were interpreted descriptively to identify performance patterns and areas for technical refinement. Result: Kinematic analysis showed coordinated joint-angle patterns across all phases. Walking analysis identified arm swing angles of 50.9°–58.8° and leg separation angles of 64.3°–67.2°, indicating a stable gait rhythm. The running analysis revealed knee angles of 68.8°–69.8° and elbow angles of 87.6°–89.1°, indicating efficient propulsive mechanics. The flight phase demonstrated knee angles of 81.2°–87.8° and elbow angles of 80.4°–88.3°, suggesting effective momentum use and postural stability. These measurements supported stride-efficiency assessment and technique evaluation. Qualitative findings revealed that Kinovea enabled athletes to interpret movement phases and identify technical inefficiencies through slow-motion and frame-by-frame visualization. Conclusion: Kinovea supports basic motion analysis by providing clear kinematic information and helping beginner athletes observe and refine their movement techniques. The findings also offer practical value for coaches by enabling more precise identification of inefficient patterns and guiding targeted corrections during early-stage training.

title: A Review of Phishing Detection Techniques Using Machine Learning and Natural Language Processing
authors: Dr. Sunita Dixit
journal: Journal of Global Research in Multidisciplinary Studies(JGRMS)
abstract: The goal of phishing attacks, which rank high among cyber risks, is to steal sensitive information (such as login passwords, financial data, and more) from unsuspecting people and companies. Blacklist, whitelist, rule, heuristic, and signature-based detection methods are no longer suitable due to the rising sophistication of phishing schemes. As a result, ML, DL, and NLP are rapidly becoming into effective instruments for detecting both well-known and brand-new forms of phishing. Background on phishing assaults, old ways of detecting them, and recent advances in intelligent phishing detection are all included in this article. It delves into several machine learning algorithms such as decision tree, LSTM, ANN, CNN, and RNN, as well as deep learning models like KNN, NB, and SVM. Also, natural language processing methods including word embedding, sentiment analysis, text categorization, and tokenization are explored with the aim of detecting phishing material. Presenting a comprehensive, precise, and up-to-the-minute phishing detection system is the ultimate goal of this study, which focuses on machine learning frameworks, performance indicators, present obstacles, and future research directions.

abstract: In the context of increasing complexity of modern network infrastructures and the growing number of cyberattacks, improving the effectiveness of intrusion detection systems is a highly relevant task. The aim of this work is to develop and investigate a hybrid approach to network attack detection based on a combination of signature-based analysis and intelligent machine learning methods.  The research methods include analysis of requirements for anomaly detection systems, comparative analysis of existing solutions, design of a hybrid system architecture, and experimental modeling using multiclass classification of network traffic. The results demonstrate that integrating a neural model with a traditional detection system improves attack detection coverage and reduces the number of false positives.  The practical significance of the study lies in the possibility of deploying the proposed architecture in real corporate networks, while the theoretical significance consists in substantiating the effectiveness of a hybrid approach to traffic analysis. Future research directions include adaptive model training and expansion of the range of detectable attacks.

title: Practical Solutions to Common TAVI Complications
authors: Herbert Kroon
abstract: Aortic valve stenosis Calcific aortic valve degeneration mainly affects the elderly population. Approximately 15% of elderly patients have some degree of aortic stenosis (AS)1. Untreated severe AS will lead to heart failure, angina and/or syncope and approximately half of patients will expire within 2 years after symptom onset1, 2. Historically, open heart surgery was the only treatment for severe AS. However, advanced age was a dominant argument to defer surgery. Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) was contrived as a less invasive alternative to surgery and to fulfill this unmet clinical need. After the first-in-human procedure in 2002, TAVI matured into a guideline recommended treatment of symptomatic severe AS in elderly patients across the entire risk spectrum3-7. Peri-procedural embolization Operator experience, improved planning and implantation strategies and multiple device iterations including smaller profile, repositioning ability and outer sealing fabric converted TAVI into a reproducible and relatively safe procedure8. However, the “Big Five” of complications in the modern TAVI era remain 1) access site complications and bleedings, 2) paravalvular leakage (PVL), 3) acute kidney injury (AKI), 4) conduction disturbances including the need for permanent pacemaker implantation (PPI) and 5) stroke9. Up to 5% of patients suffer a neurological event after TAVI, mainly within the first 48 hours8, 10, 11. This finding suggests a direct causative role with the transcatheter valve implantation itself. Transcranial Doppler and brain Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) studies revealed debris embolization towards the brain and new brain lesions after TAVI in the vast majority of patients12-15. Most of these embolizations remain clinically silent at first sight but may be linked to neurocognitive decline and frank dementia16. Embolic protection devices (EPD) have been developed to deflect or capture embolized debris on its way to the brain and may possibly reduce brain lesions and neurological events including stroke and neurocognitive decline. Part I of this thesis adds perspective to the etiopathology of TAVI related stroke and the mechanism of action of the current spectrum of cerebral embolic protection devices. We also present insights into the microscopic analysis of debris that was captured with filters during TAVI procedures. Vascular access and complications 1 TAVI typically requires large bore femoral artery access. By default, larger arteriotomies are at higher risk for access site complications and bleedings. A completely percutaneous approach relies on vascular access closure devices (VCD) to manage the arteriotomy and provide patent hemostasis. TAVI in low to intermediate risk patients is associated with a major vascular complication rate ranging between 2 and 8%4, 11. The conventional closure technique is based on sutures and most access site complications after TAVI procedures are related to closure device failure17. A collagen plug based closure device was introduced as an alternative to sutures. Part II of this thesis addresses vascular complications and provides information on clinical outcomes with collagen plug-based VCD. TAVI-related conduction disturbances Acquired conduction disturbances after TAVI are frequent and may lead to heart failure (re-) admissions and impaired long-term prognosis18-22. The atrioventricular bundle pierces the membranous septum between the right and non-coronary cusp of the aortic valve and surfaces along the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT), which makes it vulnerable to contact pressure by the implanted transcatheter heart valve (THV) during TAVI23, 24. New left bundle branch block (LBBB) and third-degree atrioventricular block (AV3B) requiring PPI occur in up to a third and quarter of patients, respectively18-22. These conduction disturbances may be transient or remain permanent which is clinically relevant in view of in-hospital stay and overall healthcare costs. Unfortunately, there are no uniform definitions to describe conduction dynamics post-TAVI. Inconsistent reporting makes the interpretation of the literature on this topic challenging. Part III of this thesis will elaborate on what is currently known about the incidence of newly acquired conduction disturbances after TAVI and studies specific features on the baseline and postprocedural electrocardiogram (ECG) to predict conduction dynamics. These insights may help determine the need and timing of PPI and adjust hospital discharge policies.

title: Incomplete atrioventricular septal defect as an incidental finding in an African lion (Panthera leo) cub during an acute multi-organ crisis: case report
authors: Sachin Patil; Utkarsh Rajhans; Aniket Mhase; Gaurav Srivastava; Navnath Nighot
abstract: Background Congenital heart defects are reported less often in non-domestic than in domestic species, although reports now span felids, primates, ungulates, and marine mammals. Atrioventricular septal defects (AVSDs), which arise from abnormal development of the endocardial cushions, are among the less frequently reported congenital heart defects in animals. Case description A 137-day-old female African lion cub (13.14 kg) was presented with generalized weakness, incoordination, dyspnea, and dehydration. Initial investigations revealed severe hypoglycemia, hemoconcentration, marked hepatocellular and muscle enzyme elevation, hyperkalemia, and an elevated cardiac troponin I concentration (8.9 ng/mL). Transthoracic echocardiography, performed after metabolic stabilization, incidentally identified a 2.2-cm defect in the primum portion of the atrial septum adjacent to the atrioventricular valves, consistent with an incomplete AVSD, with predominant left-to-right shunting and right ventricular volume overload. An agitated saline study additionally demonstrated a right-to-left shunt component. Despite supportive care, the cub developed azotemia and conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and died on day 4. Necropsy confirmed a 2 × 2.5-cm defect extending from the mid-atrial septum to the atrioventricular valves, right heart volume overload, right ventricular interstitial fibrosis, and multi-organ damage. Conclusion The incomplete AVSD in this cub was an incidental finding during a systemic illness, and its contribution to the fatal outcome cannot be determined. To the authors’ knowledge, this is the first report of an AVSD in a lion.

title: Clinical presentation, management strategies, and mortality outcomes in idiopathic aortitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Omar Hamdan; Sarah Otoom; Noureddin Abdaljaleel; Ahmad Sandouka; Hams Alsakarneh; Nour Al-Ruwaidan; Sara Qreini; Aktham El Hadid; هالة ربيع; Francisco Arias
abstract: Abstract Introduction Idiopathic Aortitis (IA) is defined as inflammation of the aortic wall, in the absence of a systemic disease or an infection. Most cases are found incidentally during repair of thoracic aortic aneurysms. Given the rarity of the disease, data on IA diagnosis and treatment are limited and derived mainly from small observational studies. This study aims to comprehensive and up-to-date synthesis of the available evidence on IA. Methods Literature search of the PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science databases was performed in late September 2025. Data regarding patients’ medical history, presentations, complications, diagnostic investigations, management and outcomes were obtained. Results A total of 58 studies were included, comprising data from 79 patients with idiopathic aortitis. The mean age was 46 ± 20 years, with a slight male predominance of 53%. Weight loss was the most frequently reported symptom (58%). Regarding management, 44% underwent exclusive surgical treatment, 31% received mixed therapy, and 25% were managed medically. Corticosteroids were utilized in 51% of cases. The overall mortality rate was 20%. Significant predictors of mortality included a younger age at presentation (18 vs. 48 years, P < 0.001) and descending aorta involvement ( P = 0.005). Conversely, corticosteroid administration ( P = 0.002) and clinical surveillance ( P < 0.001) were significantly associated with survival. Conclusion This meta-analysis highlights idiopathic aortitis as a severe condition with significant mortality whereas the administration of corticosteroids and clinical surveillance are strongly associated with survival, our findings emphasize the need for standardized, evidence-based management protocols and prospective multicenter studies to optimize patient outcomes.

title: Case Report: A potential cardiovascular safety signal during batroxobin therapy for sudden sensorineural hearing loss: a three-case series of acute myocardial infarction
authors: Xin Zhuang; Tianen Pan; 胡开宇; Qianli Zhu; Shengban You
abstract: Background Batroxobin, a defibrinogenating agent used as an adjunctive therapy for sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL), has an incompletely characterized cardiovascular safety profile. Cases We report three male patients with SSNHL who developed acute myocardial infarction (AMI) after batroxobin therapy. All three showed a precipitous fibrinogen decline (nadir: 0.48–0.75 g/L). AMI was diagnosed approximately 24–48 h after the final batroxobin dose. In Case 3, transient chest symptoms began on the day of the final dose and preceded the diagnosis of AMI the following day. Coronary angiography revealed varying degrees of underlying coronary abnormalities in all cases. One patient died of cardiogenic shock; the other two recovered after percutaneous coronary intervention. Conclusion In this case series, AMI occurred within 24–48 h after the final batroxobin administration in the context of marked fibrinogen reduction and underlying coronary abnormalities. These observations suggest a temporal association and raise a potential cardiovascular safety signal. Careful fibrinogen monitoring and individualized cardiovascular assessment may be considered in clinically appropriate patients.

title: Neonatal kidney injury: diagnosis, management, and long-term kidney health – the perspective of the European Neonatal Nephrology Working Group
authors: Lieke A. Hoogenboom; Tim Hundscheid; Evelien Snauwaert; Enrico Vidal; Natasha Su Lynn Ng; Maria Livia Ognean; Sandra Habbig; Rute Baeta Babtista; Stephanie Dufek; Genny Raffaeli; Michiel F. Schreuder; Naveen Kumar Athiraman; Eleanor J. Molloy; Johan van de Walle; Stella Stabouli; Karel Allegaert; Anke Raaijmakers; On behalf of the ESPN Working Group and ESPR Special Interest Group neonatal nephrology
abstract: Advances in perinatal and neonatal care have improved the survival of preterm and intrauterine growth-restricted (IUGR) infants, yet these achievements bring underlit challenges, including kidney development and long-term renal health. Because nephrogenesis occurs largely before birth, preterm birth interrupts this process, resulting in reduced and structurally immature nephrons. These infants, as well as those exposed to adverse intrauterine environments such as malnutrition or preeclampsia, are predisposed to kidney vulnerability that extends into later life, increasing their risk for chronic kidney disease (CKD). Paediatric nephrologists and neonatologists from the Neonatal Nephrology Working Group (WG) of the European Society for Paediatric Nephrology (ESPN) and the Special Interest Group of the European Society for Paediatric Research (ESPR) collaborated to synthesize current evidence on risk factors, mechanisms, and management of kidney injury in neonates. Key findings highlight that neonatal acute kidney injury (AKI) remains difficult to diagnose using adult-derived criteria, as creatinine-based definitions fail to account for postnatal adaptation and fluid dynamics. AKI in neonates commonly arises from multifactorial causes (i.e., perinatal asphyxia, sepsis, patent ductus arteriosus, and/or exposure to nephrotoxic drugs) and often manifests through systemic consequences like fluid overload. Management emphasizes fluid and electrolyte optimization, cautious use of nephrotoxic agents, and individualized nutrition to support growth while minimizing metabolic derangements. Emerging neonatal-specific kidney replacement therapy technologies, including miniaturized and continuous circuits, expand therapeutic options but require further evaluation. Follow-up is warranted; nevertheless, current evidence is unable to provide an evidence-based strategy. This evaluation underscores the urgent need for integrative research, neonatal-specific diagnostic criteria, and evidence-based guidelines tailored to this vulnerable population. By bridging neonatology and nephrology, the newly established WG aims to foster multidisciplinary strategies that improve both short- and long-term kidney outcomes in preterm and critically ill newborns. A higher resolution version of the Graphical abstract is available as Supplementary information

title: Delayed Stanford Type A Aortic Dissection Following Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation in a Patient With Pre-existing Ascending Aortic Dilatation
authors: Andreas Kyvetos; Stamatios Georgopoulos; Grigoris Trikas; Athanasia Detsika; Athina Mpatsouli; Sotirios Xydonas; Athanasios G. Trikas
abstract: Acute aortic dissection is an exceptionally rare but potentially fatal complication of transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI).Although most cases are recognized during or shortly after the procedure, delayed presentations following apparently uncomplicated TAVI have also been reported.An 81-year-old woman with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis and pre-existing ascending aortic dilatation of 45 mm underwent successful transfemoral TAVI with a 26-mm Hydra self-expanding transcatheter heart valve.Seven days later, she presented with sudden severe retrosternal chest pain radiating to the back and neck.Despite hemodynamic stability, a non-ischemic electrocardiogram, and normal serial high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I levels, the clinical presentation raised suspicion of acute aortic syndrome.Transthoracic echocardiography revealed an intimal flap in the ascending aorta.Emergency computed tomography angiography confirmed Stanford type A aortic dissection with associated intramural hematoma.The patient was immediately referred for emergency cardiothoracic surgery but deteriorated and died before definitive repair could be performed.Delayed aortic dissection should be considered in patients presenting with new severe chest pain after TAVI, even following an apparently uncomplicated procedure and in the presence of initially reassuring hemodynamic, electrocardiographic, and biomarker findings.Pre-existing ascending aortic dilatation may represent a vulnerable anatomical substrate and warrants careful consideration during pre-procedural assessment.A low threshold for urgent multimodality imaging is essential to facilitate early diagnosis and management of this rare but life-threatening complication.

title: Cardiovascular magnetic resonance feature-tracking strain characterization across phenotypic spectrum of danon disease
authors: Guijuan Cao; Ni Liu; Jinghui Li; Zixian Chen; Gang Yin; Weipeng Yan; Xiang Wang; Chen Cui; Minjie Lu
journal: The International Journal of Cardiovascular Imaging
abstract: To characterize atrial and ventricular strain across the phenotypic spectrum of Danon disease (DD) and explore their relationships with left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) extent. This retrospective case-control study included 27 DD patients (median age 17 [range 10-50] years; 15 males) and 32 healthy controls. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging was performed at 3-T with cine and LGE. Structural, functional, and LGE parameters were assessed. Kruskal-Wallis H test with Dunn's test and Bonferroni correction was used for intergroup comparisons; Mann-Whitney U or t-test for two-group comparisons; Spearman's correlation; and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis were used. Left atrial (LA) and right atrial (RA) strain were impaired across all DD subgroups versus controls, with LA strain impairment evident even in the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) subgroup with preserved LVEF. LV global longitudinal strain (LV-GLS) was reduced across all subgroups, whereas global circumferential strain (GCS) and global radial strain (GRS) impairment were confined to hypertrophic and dilated cardiomyopathy (HCM-DCM) and dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) subgroups. Mid-ventricular longitudinal strain was relatively preserved (P = 0.062). LGE extent correlated with GRS (all P < 0.01). Left atrial conduit strain rate (LASRe) demonstrated the best diagnostic performance (area under the curve [AUC] = 0.981; sensitivity 88.9%, specificity 100%). CMR feature-tracking revealed phenotype-specific bi-atrial and biventricular strain abnormalities in DD. Atrial strain impairment was detectable even in HCM with preserved LVEF, suggesting early mechanical dysfunction. LASRe showed promising discrimination and warrants validation. HCM-DCM may represent a possible transitional phenotype; longitudinal validation is required.

title: Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair in dynamic severe functional mitral regurgitation: A multicentre, randomised, controlled trial
authors: Bingzhen Li; Xiaojie Cai; Chao Li; Menghui Liu; Peihan Xie; Qian Zhou; Zhenyu Xiong; Cuiling Li; Fengjuan Yao; Min Ye; Wenjing Zhang; Junqi Zhong; Shaozhao Zhang; Xinxue Liao; Xiaodong Zhuang
journal: European Heart Journal - Valvular and Structural Heart Disease
abstract: Abstract Background Functional mitral regurgitation (FMR) is a highly dynamic disease. Some patients exhibit only moderate (2+) FMR at rest, which deteriorates to moderate-to-severe or severe FMR (3+ or 4+) during stress, with effective regurgitant orifice area (EROA) increased ≥0.1 cm2—termed dynamic severe FMR. Observational studies link this condition to worse outcomes, with mitral valve intervention offering potential benefits; however, high-quality evidence remains deficient. Aims The Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair In dynaMic sEvere functional mitral Regurgitation (TIMER) trial aims to assess the safety and effectiveness of transcatheter edge-to-edge repair plus guideline-directed medical therapy versus guideline-directed medical therapy alone in symptomatic chronic heart failure patients with dynamic severe FMR, defined as moderate (2+) regurgitation at rest (EROA ≥0.2 cm2 to <0.3 cm2 and/or regurgitant volume (RVol) ≥30 mL/beat to <45 mL/beat), deteriorating to moderate-to-severe or severe (3+ or 4+) during handgrip stress echocardiography (stress EROA ≥0.30 cm2 and/or RVol ≥45 mL/beat), with EROA increased ≥0.1 cm2. Methods This prospective, multicentre, randomised trial enrols patients with dynamic severe FMR confirmed by a core laboratory using handgrip stress echocardiography, across 20 participating centres in China. Patients are randomised 1:1 to transcatheter edge-to-edge repair plus medical therapy or medical therapy alone. The primary endpoint is the composite incidence of cardiovascular death and all heart failure hospitalisations during the entire follow-up period. Conclusion This trial will provide critical evidence on transcatheter edge-to-edge repair in patients with dynamic severe FMR, informing future treatment recommendations. Trial registration number: NCT07197021

title: Human‑Scale Lymphatic Modeling to Guide Lymphatic Interventions: Application to a Soft Robotic Assist Device
authors: Andreas Escher; Luca Rosalia; Elena Bosoni; Ellen Tunney Roche; Marcus Granegger
abstract: PURPOSE: The lymphatic system is essential for maintaining tissue-fluid homeostasis. In conditions of elevated venous pressures (e.g., congestive heart failure or congenital single-ventricle heart disease after Fontan palliation), increased capillary filtration and impaired lymphatic drainage disrupt this balance, predisposing patients to lymphatic overload and edema. The lack of human-scale computational models capturing lymphatic pumping and coupled tissue-fluid exchange limits the development of effective interventions. METHODS: We developed a human-scale lumped-parameter model that combines multi-lymphangion thoracic duct pumping with a Starling-based tissue-fluid balance model, enabling integrated simulation of central lymphatic function and tissue-fluid homeostasis. The framework was used to evaluate surgical and device-based lymphatic interventions. Model predictions were combined with virtual fitting using MR-derived anatomy from three Fontan patients to demonstrate translational applicability and design an extravascular soft robotic lymphatic assist sleeve, whose performance was characterized in hydraulic benchtop experiments. RESULTS: The model reproduced physiologic thoracic duct flow (~3.1L/day) and predicted interstitial fluid accumulation under venous hypertension (up to ~ 18 mL/min net accumulation). Surgical (lymphatic decompression) and device-based (extravascular sleeve) interventions increased thoracic duct flow and reduced simulated tissue-fluid accumulation (47% and 76.5% reduction, respectively), with the sleeve providing frequency-dependent augmentation. Virtual fitting confirmed anatomical feasibility of device implantation in all three Fontan patients. Benchtop testing demonstrated pressure step-ups from 5.5 to ~ 17 mmHg and flow augmentation from 2.5 to ~ 18 mL/min at actuation frequencies of 20-60 bpm. CONCLUSION: Our human-scale computational framework offers mechanistic insights into lymphatic dysfunction under elevated venous pressure and provides a platform for the design and evaluation of lymphatic interventions.

title: Association of pre-transplant right ventricular function parameters with long-term cardiovascular outcomes following kidney transplantation
authors: Cayden Lawrence; Rushda Faruk Mansuri; Reem S. Ahmed; Ava DeLonais-Parker; Zalan Shah; Yang Lyu; Ananta Sriram; James Roe; Elsa Treiber; Katherine Desanti; Krista L. Lentine; Mina Mecheal Benjamin
journal: The International Journal of Cardiovascular Imaging
abstract: The hemodynamic effects of end-stage kidney disease and associated pulmonary hypertension may impair right ventricular (RV) function and influence cardiovascular (CV) outcomes after kidney transplantation (KT). We aimed to evaluate the association between pre-transplant echocardiographic RV function parameters, including RV strain, and long-term CV outcomes following KT. In this retrospective cohort study, we included adult KT recipients at a single Midwest academic center from 2015 to 2024 who had adequate-quality pre-transplant echocardiograms and follow-up at our institution. RV function parameters included tricuspid annular systolic velocity (S'), tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE), fractional area change (FAC), RV index of myocardial performance (RIMP), and RV free wall strain measured by two-dimensional speckle-tracking echocardiography. The primary outcome was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), defined as a composite of CV death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, cerebrovascular accident, heart failure hospitalization, coronary revascularization, or sustained ventricular arrhythmias. Among 371 patients (mean age 53.5 ± 13.1 years; 56% male) followed for a median of 4.9 years (IQR, 3.1-6.4), 79 (21.2%) experienced MACE. On univariable Cox analysis, RIMP and RV strain parameters were associated with MACE, whereas S', TAPSE, and FAC were not. Kaplan-Meier analysis showed lower MACE-free survival in patients with abnormal mid and apical RV strain, whereas the basal and dichotomized average-strain comparisons were not significant. In multivariable models, only average, mid, and apical RV strain remained independently associated with MACE. Pre-transplant RV strain was independently associated with long-term MACE after KT and may aid CV risk stratification. Further studies are needed to validate these findings.

title: Association Between Colchicine Use and Clinical Outcomes Post Cardiac Surgery: A Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
authors: Vikash Jaiswal; Muhammad Hanif; Hafsa Arshad Azam Raja; Sulochana Khadka; Novonil Deb; Yusra Mashkoor; Aymen Ahmed; Kripa Rajak; Arvind Kumar Jaiswal; Mohit Gupta; Sameer A Hirji; Gregg C. Fonarow; Arman Qamar
abstract: Colchicine has been shown to mitigate inflammation and reduce adverse cardiovascular events. However, evidence from clinical trials has been mixed regarding its efficacy in cardiovascular prevention among patients undergoing cardiac surgery. We aimed to evaluate the association between colchicine use and cardiovascular outcomes in patients undergoing cardiac surgery. We conducted a systematic literature search on various electronic databases for relevant studies from their inception until July 15, 2025. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with two arms—one with colchicine as an intervention and the other with placebo—in patients undergoing cardiac surgery were included. Risk ratios (RRs) and weighted mean differences (WMDs), along with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), were pooled using a random-effects model. A p value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Nine RCTs with 2005 patients (990 in the colchicine group and 1015 in the placebo group) were included. The mean age was 62.8 years. Pooled analysis demonstrated that compared with placebo, colchicine was significantly associated with a reduction in the risk of postoperative atrial fibrillation (POAF) (RR 0.70 [95% CI 0.59–0.83], p < 0.001). However, between the groups, there was no statistically significant difference in the risk of all-cause mortality (ACM) (RR 0.81 [95% CI 0.39–1.69], p = 0.57, I 2 = 0%), stroke (RR 1.86 [95% CI 0.48–7.12], p = 0.37), and permanent pacemaker implantation (PPM) (RR 1.36 [95% CI 0.08–22.44], p = 0.83). Length of hospital stay, which was exploratory, was significantly shorter in the colchicine group (WMD – 1.16 [95% CI – 1.89 to – 0.44], p < 0.01) compared to placebo. This meta-analysis demonstrates that colchicine appears to reduce the risk of POAF. However, it does not significantly affect the risks in terms of PPM, ACM, or stroke. PROSPERO identifier no. CRD420251117966.

title: Sealed Post-infarction Left Ventricular Free-Wall Rupture in a Patient Taking Dabigatran: A Case Report
authors: Raffaele Carluccio; Amalia Siracusa; Giuseppe Cioffi; Crescenzo Testa; Fabio Minicucci
abstract: Left ventricular free-wall rupture is a rare but life-threatening mechanical complication of acute myocardial infarction.In its subacute form, thrombus and pericardium temporarily contain the bleeding, opening a narrow window for diagnosis and surgery.We report a 76-year-old man with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation treated with dabigatran and with impaired renal function, who presented with syncope and cardiogenic shock after five days of untreated chest pain.The electrocardiogram (ECG) showed ST-segment elevation with QS complexes in leads I and aVL and reciprocal depression in the inferior leads, a pattern typical of first diagonal branch occlusion.Bedside echocardiography revealed a large, organized hemopericardium, and CT excluded aortic dissection.Coronary angiography confirmed occlusion of the first diagonal branch.Antithrombotic loading was withheld.At emergency surgery, a 1 × 1 cm tear of the mid-lateral free wall, matching the culprit territory, was found already sealed by thrombus; it was repaired with a sutureless patch technique combined with off-pump internal mammary artery grafting.After surgical re-exploration for recurrent postoperative bleeding, the patient recovered and was alive at 18 months.This case highlights the value of electrocardiographic localization, the central role of bedside echocardiography, and the practical issues raised by a direct oral anticoagulant at the time of rupture.

title: SYNERGISTIC ANTIOXIDANT AND ANTI-INFLAMMATORY ACTIVITIES OF N-ACETYLCYSTEINE AND GLUTATHIONE EVALUATED THROUGH IN SILICO AND IN VITRO APPROACHES
authors: Gundeti Tharun Reddy; LANKAPOTHU PREM BALAJI REDDY; SRINIVASAN MK; Sakthivel Muthu
journal: Asian Journal of Pharmaceutical and Clinical Research
abstract: Objectives: Oxidative stress and inflammation are interconnected pathological mechanisms implicated in the initiation and progression of several chronic disorders. Natural antioxidant molecules, such as N-acetylcysteine (NAC) and glutathione (GSH) possess potential therapeutic benefits; however, their combined effects require further investigation. This study aimed to evaluate the antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities of NAC and GSH individually and as a 1:2 combination using integrated in silico and in vitro approaches. Methods: The pharmacokinetic and safety profiles of NAC and GSH were predicted using computational absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) and StopTox-based toxicity analyses. The anti-inflammatory potential was assessed through egg albumin and bovine serum albumin (BSA) protein denaturation assays. Antioxidant activity was evaluated using 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH), 2,2’-azino-bis(3-ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulfonic acid (ABTS), ferric reducing antioxidant power (FRAP), and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) scavenging assays. The activities of individual compounds and the NAC: GSH combination was compared with standard antioxidants, including aspirin and ascorbic acid. Results: ADME predictions indicated that NAC exhibited favorable drug-like properties, including low molecular weight, moderate polarity, and low predicted cytochrome P450 interactions, whereas GSH showed higher polarity and reduced membrane permeability. StopTox predictions suggested that both compounds were unlikely to cause acute toxicity via oral, inhalation, or dermal exposure. The NAC: GSH combination demonstrated superior anti-inflammatory activity compared with individual treatments, showing IC50 values of 26.1 μM and 18.31 μM in egg albumin and BSA denaturation assays, respectively. Similarly, the combined formulation showed enhanced antioxidant activity, with lower IC50 values in the DPPH (35.1 μM), ABTS (30.67 μM), and FRAP (28.71 μM) assays than NAC or GSH alone. Although aspirin and ascorbic acid showed the highest overall activity among tested samples, the NAC: GSH combination displayed marked synergistic effects. Conclusion: The combined administration of NAC and GSH enhances antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities through complementary mechanisms, including NAC-mediated GSH regeneration, GSH-mediated protein stabilization, and efficient reactive oxygen species scavenging. These findings support the potential of NAC: GSH combination therapy as a promising intervention for oxidative stress- and inflammation-associated disorders. Further in vivo investigations are warranted to validate its therapeutic efficacy.

title: In Vitro Hemodynamic Assessment of a Novel Pulmonary Visceral Pleura (PVP) Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement Prototype Based on Optical and Acoustic Measurements
authors: Colten Alme; Santu Golder; Xiao Lu; Haoxiang Luo; Yan Zhang
abstract: Structural valve degradation remains a key limitation of bioprosthetic transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) devices, whose bovine or porcine pericardium leaflets are prone to calcification and long-term failure. Pulmonary visceral pleura (PVP), a thin, elastin-rich tissue, has emerged as a promising alternative leaflet material. This study presents an in vitro hemodynamic evaluation of a prototype PVP valve under physiologically representative pulsatile flow in a custom benchtop flow loop. A multimodal framework combined four techniques: high-speed imaging with U-Net deep learning segmentation of the geometric orifice area, quantitative Doppler velocity extraction developed on a Verasonics research ultrasound platform, double-pulse particle image velocimetry (PIV) of the downstream flow field, and transvalvular pressure measurement. The PVP valve was compared with a stiff silicone valve representing a stenotic reference condition. At 75 bpm and 5 L/min, the PVP valve reached a peak geometric orifice area of 2.91 cm2, a mean pressure gradient of 4.3 mmHg, and a peak jet velocity of 2.46 m/s, meeting the ASE velocity and gradient criteria for normal prosthetic valve function. The silicone valve opened to 1.1 cm2 with a gradient of 36.9 mmHg, consistent with moderate-to-severe stenosis. The framework provides a basis for characterizing new bioprosthetic valve materials and benchmark data for fluid–structure interaction modeling.

title: Engineered synbiotic microspheres enable system-level reprogramming of the gut-immune-vascular axis in chronic inflammatory vascular disease.
authors: Lin Shen; Mengqian Zhai; Zhangyu Yang; Junchao Yu; Ziyu Pang; Zijian Fang; Xingru Ding; Jiahui Xu; Yingtao Hu; Shiji Fang; Gaofeng Shu; Yang Yang; Lingchun Lv; S. Zhang; Jian Xu; Jianhua Wu; Weiqian Chen; Chenying Lu; Minjiang Chen; Jiansong Ji
abstract: Chronic inflammatory vascular diseases are increasingly recognized as systemic disorders sustained by maladaptive cross-organ immunometabolic coupling, yet current therapeutic strategies remain largely lesion-centered and fail to address upstream drivers of disease persistence. Here, we identify the gut-immune-vascular axis as a system-level pathogenic unit that integrates gut microbial dysbiosis, intestinal barrier dysfunction, metabolic imbalance, and vascular immune activation into a self-reinforcing pathological circuit. Through integrated clinical profiling and cross-species validation, we demonstrate that disruption of this axis is characterized by coordinated probiotic depletion, expansion of proinflammatory taxa, translocation of microbial endotoxins, accumulation of microbiota-derived metabolites, and macrophage polarization toward a proinflammatory phenotype along the gut-vascular continuum. To therapeutically target this axis, we engineer enzyme-responsive synbiotic microspheres that codeliver probiotics, a microbial metabolic pathway inhibitor, and a prebiotic within a protective polymeric matrix, enabling site-specific intestinal activation and coordinated microbiota-metabolic modulation. This engineered system restores intestinal barrier integrity, reprograms microbial ecology and metabolite output, suppresses immunometabolic dysfunction, and robustly attenuates pathological vascular remodeling across cellular, murine, and large-animal models, with in-stent restenosis serving as a representative disease context. Collectively, this work establishes axis-oriented immunometabolic reprogramming as a generalizable therapeutic paradigm and highlights engineered synbiotic platforms as scalable tools for system-level intervention in chronic inflammatory diseases.

title: Contemporary Updates in Lung Transplantation: a Perioperative and Critical Care Anesthesiology Perspective
authors: Jennifer Boleyn; Christina Anne Jelly; Frederick W. Lombard; Anna Eid; John Bryant
abstract: Abstract Purpose of Review This review reports advances from the past five years in the perioperative and critical care management of lung transplantation, emphasizing donor pool expansion, selection of intraoperative mechanical support, ventilation of the allograft, and mitigation of primary graft dysfunction. Recent Findings Ex vivo lung perfusion and donation after circulatory death, with normothermic regional perfusion, have enlarged the usable donor pool. Observational data and 2026 consensus statements favor venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation over cardiopulmonary bypass when intraoperative support is required, although those data cannot evaluate a planned routine support strategy. Ventilation of the allograft is becoming graft-specific rather than borrowed from acute respiratory distress syndrome practice, and enhanced recovery pathways with regional analgesia are being applied across the perioperative continuum. Summary Perioperative anesthesia management materially influences lung transplant outcomes. Priorities for future work include standardized intraoperative extracorporeal membrane oxygenation protocols, individualized ventilation, opioid-sparing analgesia, and prevention of chronic lung allograft dysfunction.

title: CT and MRI in periprocedural transcatheter mitral valve replacement: expert recommendations by the European Society of Cardiovascular Radiology (ESCR) and the North American Society for Cardiovascular Imaging (NASCI)
authors: Anna Palmisano; Marco Francone; Prabhakar Shantha Rajiah; Jonathon Leipsic; Gudrun Maria Feuchtner; Matthias Eberhard; Ricardo P.J. Budde; Bradley D. Allen; Hatem Alkadhi; Antonio Esposito
abstract: Transcatheter mitral valve replacement (TMVR) is a minimally invasive treatment option for symptomatic patients with severe mitral valve disease who are at high surgical risk or ineligible for open-heart surgery. The procedure has been associated with improved quality of life and functional status in selected patients and is increasingly recognized as a valuable therapeutic option in the management of complex mitral valve disorders. A multidisciplinary Heart Team is essential to ensure the clinical success of TMVR, and imaging specialists play a central role in the preprocedural assessment for patient and device selection, during the procedure, to guide and monitor the implantation, and after the procedure, for follow-up and for the correct diagnosis of short- or long-term complications. Echocardiography is required for initial diagnosis, for assessment of valve hemodynamics, intraprocedural guidance and monitoring. However, a multimodality approach including CT and/or MRI is frequently needed to correctly manage the phase of preprocedural planning and the diagnosis of complications. This consensus document, developed by a working group of experts from the European Society of Cardiovascular Radiology (ESCR) and the North American Society for Cardiovascular Imaging (NASCI), provides evidence-based recommendations for CT and cardiac MRI acquisition and post-processing in procedural planning and postprocedural evaluation in patients undergoing TMVR. Emphasis is placed on the technical requirements and standardization of imaging protocols, which must account for the heterogeneity of imaging equipment used in clinical settings. The document also outlines recommendations for all necessary preprocedural measures to ensure consistency, accuracy, and effective communication among specialists. KEY POINTS: Question How can CT and MRI acquisition, measurement, and reporting for TMVR be standardized to support accurate procedural planning, device selection, and follow-up? Findings This expert consensus provides recommendations for standardized CT and MRI protocols, key measurements, and structured reporting throughout TMVR planning and follow-up. Clinical relevance CT and MRI assessment may improve patient selection, procedural planning, multidisciplinary communication, and detection of postprocedural complications, supporting safer and more consistent TMVR practice across centers.

title: Nowe mechanizmy uczestniczące w modyfikacji parametrów skrzepu fibrynowego i generacji trombiny u pacjentów z niewydolnością serca
